Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
k=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor,
\]

so

\[
k^2\le n\le (k+1)^2-1.
\]

We need

\[
n\mid (k!)^{n!}+450.
\]

---

### 1. Prime powers of \(n\) whose prime is \(\le k\)

Suppose \(q^a\parallel n\) with \(q\le k\). Then \(q\mid k!\), so

\[
v_q\bigl((k!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!\,v_q(k!)\ge n!.
\]

Also \(a=v_q(n)\le n\le n!\). Hence

\[
q^a\mid (k!)^{n!}.
\]

Therefore, modulo \(q^a\),

\[
(k!)^{n!}+450\equiv 450.
\]

Since \(q^a\mid n\) and \(n\) divides the whole expression, we must have

\[
q^a\mid 450.
\]

Thus the part of \(n\) made of prime factors \(\le k\) must divide

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

---

### 2. Prime factors of \(n\) larger than \(k\)

Let \(p>k\) be a prime divisor of \(n\). Then \(p\nmid k!\). Also \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(k!)^{p-1}\equiv 1\pmod p,
\]

so because \(p-1\mid n!\),

\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Thus

\[
0\equiv (k!)^{n!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\pmod p.
\]

So

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Hence the only possible prime factors of \(n\) larger than \(k\) are \(11\) and \(41\).

Also, since \(p>k\), we have \(p\ge k+1\). Therefore \(p^2\ge (k+1)^2>n\), so such a prime can occur only to the first power, and there can be at most one such prime.

Thus \(n\) has the form

\[
n=D
\]

or

\[
n=pD,
\]

where \(D\mid 450\), and if \(p\) is present then \(p\in\{11,41\}\) and \(p>k\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

If there is no prime factor \(>k\), then

\[
n\mid 450,
\]

so \(n\le 450\).

If \(p=11\), then \(p>k\), so \(k\le 10\), hence

\[
n\le 11^2-1=120.
\]

Since \(n=11D\) and \(D\mid 450\), we get \(D\le 10\). The largest divisor of \(450\) at most \(10\) is \(10\), giving

\[
n\le 11\cdot 10=110.
\]

If \(p=41\), then \(p>k\), so

\[
n\le 41^2-1=1680.
\]

Thus \(41D\le 1680\), so \(D\le 40\). The largest divisor of \(450\) at most \(40\) is \(30\), giving

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Therefore every valid \(n\) satisfies

\[
n\le 1230.
\]

---

### 4. Check \(n=1230\)

For \(n=1230\),

\[
\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

First, \(35!\) is divisible by \(450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\), so

\[
(35!)^{1230!}
\]

is divisible by \(450\). Since \(450\) is also divisible by \(450\), their sum is divisible by \(450\), hence divisible by \(30\).

Now work modulo \(41\). Since \(35!\) is not divisible by \(41\), and \(1230!\) is divisible by \(40\), Fermat’s little theorem gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Also,

\[
450\equiv 40\equiv -1\pmod{41}.
\]

Thus

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

So the expression is divisible by both \(30\) and \(41\), and since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), it is divisible by

\[
30\cdot 41=1230.
\]

Therefore \(n=1230\) works, and no larger \(n\) can work.

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
